claims.text: The new simulation approach separately models lattice and electronic thermal-transport contributions.
Phonon transport is modeled using molecular dynamics with DFT-derived elastic properties and force constants.
The new approach will predict the lattice thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than earlier Debye-based aggregate estimates.
The modeled HfNbTaTiZr is defect-free, homogeneously mixed, and crystalline.
Independent calculations of lattice dynamics and electronic properties allow separate estimates of lattice and electronic conductivity.
The proposed applicability range is approximately 100–1200 K.
Below 200 K, lattice contributions are more discernible.
Oxygen-free specimens avoid impurity scattering associated with oxygen contamination.
Variations in atomic force constants and mass distribution mediate phonon scattering and lattice vibrational modes.
Atomistic simulation captures anharmonic lattice dynamics while electronic structure is treated independently.
Independent treatment of lattice and electronic transport avoids conflated conductivity estimates.
Predicted lattice thermal conductivity will agree with low-temperature measurements within approximately ±15%.
The new method will reduce prediction errors by approximately 20–30% relative to Debye-temperature-based approaches.
At higher temperatures, the predicted lattice contribution will be distinctly lower than total measured conductivity because electronic conduction becomes significant.
Earlier analytical approaches use a combined Debye-temperature estimate to predict overall conductivity without explicitly separating lattice and electronic components.
Predictive accuracy is expected to apply to high-purity, defect-free samples without significant oxygen contamination.
Reliability may decrease above 1200 K or in samples containing extrinsic scattering centers.
Above 1200 K, more pronounced anharmonic effects may reduce the method's reliability.

contradictions.description: The conditions say lattice contributions are merely more discernible below 200 K, whereas the experiment invokes low-temperature methods that favor lattice-dominated heat transfer. These are not equivalent, and the latter assumption is not established.
The predicted ±15% agreement is framed specifically around low-temperature measurements, but the falsification rule requires this accuracy over the entire 100–1200 K measured range.
